ch10 - 1. More Golems around Than You Might Think.md
chapters.relation: Using Feet of Clay and Witches Abroad, Froehlich argues we are all like golems: our behavior is driven by the 'words in our heads,' the texts that society and the powerful put there. Lyotard's metanarratives explain how Lily Weatherwax forces Genua to live out fairy-tale plots and how Dragon King of Arms rewrites Nobby's family tree to manufacture a king, while dwarfish gender norms keep Cheery Littlebottom trapped in a culturally imposed text. Freedom comes only when, like Dorfl after Carrot buys him his own receipt, a person rejects the imposed words and chooses words of the heart - 'words in the heart cannot be taken.'

chapters.file: ch11 - 2. Golem Morality in the Modern World.md
chapters.relation: Skene weighs Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' - opened with a River Ankh drowning-child variant - against the golem morality of Going Postal and Feet of Clay. Mr. Pump's charge that Moist von Lipwig's frauds 'hastened the deaths' of 2.338 people grounds a golem standard of actuarial murder that Skene applies to the 2008 banking crisis and Mao's Great Leap Forward. With Kant, the chapter holds that free choice is the foundation of moral responsibility and respect for others' wills, but unlike Singer's unlimited demands, golem morality asks us to own the foreseeable consequences of our choices without sacrificing everything.

chapters.file: ch12 - 3. We Willna Be Fooled Again! Wee Free Anarchists!.md
chapters.relation: Reading The Wee Free Men, Kugler treats the Nac Mac Feegle, Granny Aching, and Tiffany as embodiments of the anarchist suspicion of political authority, staging Nozick's minimal state and spontaneous protective associations against Huemer's philosophical anarchism from The Problem of Political Authority. The Feegles' creed 'Nae quin! Nae king!', their flight from the exploitative Fairy Queen, the Baron's sheep-killing dog compromise, and the mercy shown the lonely kidnapper Miss Robinson all show law treated as a flexible guideline that must yield to love, community, and care for the weak. Kugler concludes that Pratchett romanticizes anarchism: his anarchists win hearts, watching authority from within the system rather than overthrowing it.

chapters.file: ch13 - 4. The Liberating Power of Nanny Ogg’s Bouncing Bosom.md
chapters.relation: Froehlich reads Witches Abroad through Mikhail Bakhtin's theory of carnival and the grotesque from Rabelais and His World: Lily Weatherwax's palace ball is 'high culture' as tyrannical hierarchy, while the Genua street carnival, Nanny Ogg's bouncing bosom, and Baron Saturday's untamable swamp bring grotesque low-culture energy that crashes the ball and shatters Lily's frozen fairy-tale order. Against Bakhtin's pessimism that carnival merely lets the oppressed blow off steam, the chapter argues that Granny Weatherwax and Nanny break the cycle, giving Genua a real chance at self-determined, more fun lives.

chapters.file: ch14 - 5. The Truth Shall Make Ye Fret.md
chapters.relation: Watson uses The Truth - William de Worde's accidental invention of Ankh-Morpork's first newspaper and the plot to frame Lord Vetinari - to stage the three classic arguments for censorship: direct harm (character assassination 'works every day'), indirect harm (with MacKinnon's point that the speech of the dominant drowns out the subordinated, applied to speciesist insults at Koom Valley), and the false-beliefs argument. Against them stand the knowledge problem and the equality assumption: Mrs. Arcanum's deference to print, Vetinari's turtle-shaped-world joke, and the Montessori-Broca dispute show we never know in advance which beliefs are false, and any censor like Lord de Worde has his own agenda. Vetinari's verdict that 'free men pull in all kinds of directions' because 'pulling together is the aim of despotism' carries the chapter's Millian case that free speech is a horrible necessity.

chapters.file: ch15 - II. Truth, Logic, and Law Are Nice, but Someone Still Has to Do the Wash.md
ch16 - 6. The Absurdity of the Luggage.md
chapters.relation: Kempner reads the Luggage - the sapient, homicidal pearwood chest that pursues Rincewind from The Color of Magic through The Light Fantastic and Interesting Times - as the embodiment of Camus's absurd: the 'divorce' between our demand that the world make sense and a world that does not care. Rincewind, who dreams of a rational, scientifically ordered universe while the Disc sails on a turtle and the gods smash atheists' windows, is cast as Sisyphus, and the trolls who 'suffer from philosophy' and freeze solid show where the futile quest for order ends. When Rincewind finally says 'Come on' to the huddled Luggage and readers come to love what once terrified them, the chapter performs Camus's acceptance of the absurd as freedom.

chapters.file: ch17 - 7. Pratchett’s Republic.md
chapters.relation: Kempner maps Plato's Republic onto Ankh-Morpork: Vetinari is the Philosopher King, the Watch of Guards! Guards! are the Guardians who devote themselves to the good of the whole community, and Platonic justice as keeping everything in its right place is Vetinari's guild-licensing, topiary-tending rule - including the jail cell whose locks are all on the inside. Against Plato's banishment of poets, The Truth shows words serving the just city: William de Worde's pursuit of 'the big truth' exposes the frame-up of Vetinari and extends the circle of Guardians to the free press. The chapter concludes that Pratchett keeps Plato's ideal only by bending it to observable reality - Vetinari rules for the city rather than remaking its people.

chapters.file: ch18 - 8. Honesty Trumps Cleverness Sam Vimes and Commonsense Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Skene argues Sam Vimes embodies Thomas Reid's common sense philosophy across Feet of Clay, Thud!, Night Watch, and Jingo: he refuses speculation (his hatred of Holmes-style clue-deduction and the Summoning Dark), is irreverent toward false authorities from Sergeant Colon's 'School of My Dad Always Said' to Lord Rust's glorious wars, and checks every theory against reality. Moore's here-is-one-hand reply to Humean skepticism and Socrates' unmasking of pompous authorities illustrate the method, and Huemer's political realism - taxation as demanded money with menaces, social systems judged by how they work for real people - echoes Vimes's verdicts on Reg Shoe's utopian barricade and Swing's phrenology. The lesson is Vimes's own: 'Common sense and facts! That's what works.'

chapters.file: ch19 - 9. Why Would You Put a Con Artist in Charge of the Money.md
chapters.relation: Fallis asks why Vetinari puts the con artist Moist von Lipwig in charge of the Post Office, Royal Bank, and Mint in Going Postal and Making Money. Analyzing what counterfeits are - Goodman's 'false history of production' definition, its failures, and bald-faced cases like Mr. Bent's deliberately transparent 'family heirlooms' lie - explains why it takes a thief to catch a thief, while the John Law affair (with Kant's observation that Law escaped France without ever lying) supplies the cautionary precedent. The deepest answer is Searle's: money is an institutional fact, a collective agreement that X counts as Y, so only a con artist skilled at 'selling dreams' can talk Ankh-Morpork's merchants into accepting paper.

chapters.file: ch20 - 10. Lord Vetinari’s Friendly Guide to Tyranny.md
chapters.relation: Alloy stages the debate over Vetinari's legitimacy as letters to the Ankh-Morpork Times: a writer channeling Hobbes defends the contracted sovereign - a 'mortal god' who cannot commit crimes and secures freedom through security - while 'the late Jeremy Bentham' judges the Patrician by the greatest good of the greatest number yet would disenfranchise golems and the 'differently-alive' dead. The anarchist Wolff Paul Roberts rebuts both, denying any right to rule, rejecting tacit consent by residence, and holding up the free golems as models of uncoerced virtue, before a final letter defends Vetinari's limited, functional government. The frame - Vetinari quietly orchestrating the whole correspondence and planning Roberts's next letter - shows tyranny curating its own philosophical defense.

chapters.file: ch21 - III. Some Things are Necessary, Not Personal.md
ch22 - 11. Can a Leopard Change Its Shorts.md
chapters.relation: Alloy asks whether Rincewind - the wizard who runs from Twoflower, the Dungeon Dimensions, and the Agatean Empire alike - is really a coward. Aristotle's doctrine of the mean frames cowardice as the deficiency of fear-regulation between foolhardy Cohen the Barbarian and true courage, with character traits describing, explaining, and predicting Rincewind's flight. But the situationist challenge - Harman's reading of the cookie, hurry, and obedience experiments - denies that character traits exist, and the replies available to the virtue ethicist (Miller's continence/incontinence distinction, Alfano's 'dodge') leave almost nobody with virtues or vices, so the chapter concludes Rincewind cannot be a coward: cowardice, like the leopard's shorts, was never there to begin with.

chapters.file: ch23 - 12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld.md
chapters.relation: Pierce uses Moist von Lipwig's rehabilitation (Albert Spangler becomes Postmaster General), Cosmo Lavish's doomed project of literally becoming Vetinari, the Auditor Myria LeJean, Angua's transformations, the Librarian's orangutan body, Miss Level's two bodies, and duplicated Rincewind teleportation cases to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory theory, patched by Leibniz into psychological continuity, collapses into circularity under false-memory cases like a wizard implanting Teatime's murders in Rincewind's mind, while bodily and brain-continuity views founder on Igor part-swaps, splitting hemispheres, and identical-twin-style fission. Leibniz's own soul view and Reid's treatment of identity as a primitive, unanalyzable fact get their due, and Hume's skepticism about any continuing self marks the chapter's conclusion that every available view exacts a price.

holes.name: Michael Huemer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose The Problem of Political Authority argues that the state has no special moral authority and defends philosophical anarchism.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Huemer's anarchism as the modern foil to Nozick's minimal state in reading the Nac Mac Feegle's contempt for all political authority.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian thinker whose Rabelais and His World theorizes carnival and the grotesque body as popular inversions of official high culture and social hierarchy.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Nanny Ogg, the Genua carnival, and Baron Saturday in Witches Abroad directly through Bakhtin's carnival/grotesque theory.

holes.name: Michael Huemer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose The Problem of Political Authority argues that the state has no special moral authority and defends philosophical anarchism.
holes.why: Chapter 18 builds its section on Vimes's political realism - taxation as coercion, anti-utopianism, the psychology of submitting to authority - on Huemer's book.

holes.name: Nelson Goodman
holes.what: Philosopher whose Languages of Art defines counterfeits as objects falsely purporting to have the requisite history of production, and inventor of the 'grue' paradox.
holes.why: Chapter 19 tests and revises Goodman's definition of the counterfeit to explain how Moist von Lipwig secures Ankh-Morpork's banknotes and stamps against forgery.

holes.name: Institutional Facts (social reality)
holes.what: Searle's account of how collective agreement ('X counts as Y in context C') creates social realities such as money, borders, and games.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues paper currency works only because Moist cons Ankh-Morpork's merchants into collectively accepting slips of paper as money, which is Searle's institutional-fact machinery applied.

holes.name: The Situationist Challenge to Character
holes.what: The social-psychology-based thesis (associated with Harman and Doris) that behavior is driven by situational factors rather than stable character traits, undermining virtue ethics.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Rincewind cannot be a coward because the situationist challenge shows there are no character traits such as courage or cowardice to have.
